% fractions — a stacked fraction read as one quantity rather than two lines.
%
% One concern: two baselines with a rule between them mean 𝑎 divided by 𝑏, and read as
% text they are 𝑎 and 𝑏 separated by whatever the wrap inferred. Extracting this document
% before joinFractions existed gave "12 116", which is not a formula that is hard to read —
% it is a different formula, and nothing in the output says which one the page set.
%
% Built with pdflatex, and that is the point rather than the convention. pdfTeX *strokes* a
% fraction bar — "0.398 w x y m x y l S", one rule with no second edge anywhere on the
% page — where ISO 32000-2 *fills* a rectangle and so emits both of its long edges. A
% reader that recovers thickness only from a pair of edges finds every fraction in the ISO
% documents and none here, which is exactly the state this file was written to catch. Every
% fraction in the corpus lives in a gitignored PDF, so without this fixture a clone runs no
% end-to-end fraction test at all.
%
% Display math, not inline. An inline \frac sets its levels in scriptstyle around the text
% baseline, and the prose on that baseline then lies *between* the numerator and the
% denominator — so the two levels are not adjacent line records and the rewrite cannot see
% them. Measured on this file's own text, "An inline fraction $\frac{12}{116}$ sits in a
% sentence" extracts as "An inline fraction 1", "2", "116 sits in a sentence": the levels
% are not joined and the numerator is split across two lines. That is a real limitation,
% logged as one; it is not what this fixture is for, and a fixture asserting it would be
% pinning the wrong output. Every fraction the corpus has is set the way these are, with
% each level alone on its own line.
%
% The three equations are chosen for what separates them:
%
%   - 12 over 116 is the simple case, and the only one whose bar has an extent of its own.
%   - (1 + 2) over 3 needs the parentheses. ISO 80000-2 requires them when a level is a sum
%     or a difference, because the solidus binds tighter than the "+" above it: "1 + 2/3"
%     is a different number.
%   - 12 over (3 + 4) takes them on the other side, and its bar is *the same extent as the
%     equation above it* — 294.554 to 316.693 in both, because "1 + 2" and "3 + 4" set to
%     the same width in this font. That collision is the reason this equation is here.
%     Deciding a grid line by "has a parallel partner at this extent" made these two
%     fractions cancel each other, and a page that sets the same formula twice draws it.
%     Three rules at one extent are a table; two are a coincidence.
%
% The horizontal rule below the equations is the negative case, and it is the most common
% false positive the corpus has: two prose paragraphs with a full-width rule between them,
% which is a mark between two baselines with text above and below it, the same shape a
% fraction bar has. It is declined on overhang — the rule reaches far past the wider line,
% where a bar is drawn for the expression it divides and exceeds it by a typesetter's
% margin. The gold file asserts that it contributes no solidus and no text, so a rule that
% took it would fail here rather than in a corpus count nobody reads.
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lmodern}
\pagestyle{empty}

\begin{document}

A stacked fraction is two baselines with a rule between them, and on the page it means one
quantity.

\[ \frac{12}{116} \]

The numerator is a sum, so the solidus form needs it bracketed.

\[ \frac{1 + 2}{3} \]

The denominator is a sum, and takes the brackets on the other side. Its bar is drawn at the
same extent as the bar above it.

\[ \frac{12}{3 + 4} \]

The rule below this paragraph divides nothing, and is the shape a fraction bar has.

\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}

It reaches far past both lines it sits between, where a bar is drawn for the expression it
divides.

\end{document}
